lessons.title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
lessons.description: What affects reaction speed, how collision theory explains it, catalysts and core practical methods.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Rate of Reaction?

The rate of reaction measures how quickly a chemical reaction proceeds. It is calculated using:

$$\text{rate of reaction} = \frac{\text{quantity of reactant used or product formed}}{\text{time taken}}$$

The ‘quantity’ can be measured as mass (g), volume of gas (cm3), or by monitoring a colour change. The four main factors that affect rate are: temperature, concentration (or gas pressure), surface area of solids, and the use of a catalyst.

Key Fact

Rate of reaction increases with: higher temperature, greater concentration (or pressure for gases), greater surface area, and the presence of a catalyst. It can be measured by: collecting gas produced, monitoring mass loss, or timing a colour change.

Collision Theory

Collision theory explains why these factors affect rate. For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with each other and that collision must have enough energy to overcome the activation energy. Any change that increases the frequency of successful collisions increases the rate.

Temperature: higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy. They move faster, collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy. Even a small temperature rise can dramatically increase rate.

Concentration / Pressure: a higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so particles are closer together and collide more often. For gases, increasing pressure has the same effect — it compresses the gas and raises particle density.

Surface area: breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more surface for reactant particles to collide with. The total volume of solid is unchanged but more of it is accessible, so collisions are more frequent.

Catalyst: provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. At any given temperature, a larger fraction of collisions now have enough energy to react, so the rate increases. The catalyst is not consumed.

Core Practical — Measuring Rates of Reaction

Your course includes a core practical investigating how factors affect the rate of reaction. Two standard methods are used:

Marble chips (calcium carbonate) react with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce carbon dioxide gas:

$$CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2$$

Rate is measured by collecting the gas in a gas syringe and recording the volume every 30 seconds. The independent variable (e.g. concentration of acid, or surface area of chips) is changed; the dependent variable is the volume of CO2 produced over time. Control variables include: mass of marble chips, temperature, total volume of solution.

The initial gradient of a volume-vs-time graph gives the initial rate. Steeper gradients indicate faster rates. Each experiment should be repeated to check reproducibility and calculate a mean.

When sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, a yellow precipitate of sulfur forms:

$$Na_2S_2O_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow 2NaCl + H_2O + SO_2 + S$$

Rate is measured by placing the flask over a cross drawn on white paper and timing how long it takes for the cross to disappear as the sulfur cloud builds up. A shorter time means a faster rate. The independent variable is concentration (or temperature); the dependent variable is time for cross to disappear. Control variables: volume of solutions, room temperature, the same cross viewed from the same height.

Rate can then be expressed as \(\frac{1}{\text{time}}\) — this makes comparison easier as a larger value corresponds to a faster rate.

Key Fact

Both core practical methods require clear identification of: independent variable (what you change), dependent variable (what you measure), and control variables (everything else kept constant). Examiners look for repeats and a method of calculating rate from collected data.

Interpreting Rate Graphs

A graph of product formed against time produces a curve that starts steep and levels off as reactants are used up. The steeper the initial gradient, the faster the initial rate. When the line is horizontal, the reaction has stopped. Comparing two experiments on the same axes, the one with the steeper initial gradient has the faster rate — caused by higher temperature, greater concentration, greater surface area, or the presence of a catalyst.

For calculation questions, if rate is defined as 1/time, a shorter time means a faster rate. When drawing graphs of volume of gas against time, the steeper the initial gradient, the faster the rate. Catalysts and higher temperatures both produce steeper gradients without changing the final total volume of product obtained at completion, because the same amount of reactant is consumed in both cases.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For core practical questions, always state the independent variable, dependent variable, and at least two control variables. When asked to explain why rate increases with temperature, give the full collision theory answer: particles gain more kinetic energy, move faster, collide more frequently AND a greater proportion of collisions exceed the activation energy. Giving only one of these two reasons is a common way to lose the second mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rate of reaction is increased by raising temperature, increasing concentration or pressure, increasing surface area, or adding a catalyst. Collision theory explains each: more frequent or more energetic collisions mean more successful reactions per second.
  • The core practical uses two methods: marble chips + HCl (gas syringe, measure CO₂ volume) and sodium thiosulfate + HCl (cross timing, measure how long for precipitate to obscure the cross).
  • On rate graphs, a steeper initial gradient means a faster rate. The reaction stops when the line becomes flat (one reactant is used up).

lessons.title: Reversible Reactions, Equilibrium and the Haber Process
lessons.description: Reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle and the Haber process.
lessons.content_html:
Reversible Reactions

Some chemical reactions can proceed in both directions. In a reversible reaction, the products can react together to re-form the original reactants. These reactions are represented using a double arrow (\(\rightleftharpoons\)) rather than a single arrow. A straightforward example is the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride:

$$NH_4Cl \rightleftharpoons NH_3 + HCl$$

Heating drives the forward reaction; cooling drives the reverse. The energy is conserved: if the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic by exactly the same amount.

Key Fact

In a reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic by the same amount of energy — and vice versa.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system (nothing enters or leaves), it eventually reaches dynamic equilibrium. At equilibrium:

  • The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
  • The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (they are not necessarily equal).
  • Both reactions are still happening — equilibrium is dynamic, not static. The reaction has not stopped.
Key Fact

At dynamic equilibrium, both forward and reverse reactions continue at the same rate. Concentrations stay constant because the rate of product formation equals the rate of product being converted back to reactants. The reaction has NOT stopped.

Le Chatelier’s Principle

Le Chatelier’s principle states: if conditions are changed in a system at equilibrium, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes the change.

Temperature: increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction (absorbs the extra heat). Decreasing temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction (releases heat to compensate). Temperature is the only factor that changes the value of the equilibrium constant.

Concentration: increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium to the right (forward reaction) to use up the extra reactant. Increasing the concentration of a product shifts equilibrium to the left.

Pressure (gases only): increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas, to reduce the pressure. Decreasing pressure shifts it towards the side with more moles of gas.

The Haber Process

The Haber process manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen:

$$N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3 \quad (\Delta H = -92 \text{ kJ/mol})$$

The forward reaction is exothermic. The nitrogen comes from the air; the hydrogen is obtained mainly from natural gas (methane). The reaction is carried out at approximately 450°C and 200 atmospheres pressure, using a finely divided iron catalyst.

Temperature — rate vs yield: the forward reaction is exothermic. Lowering temperature would favour the forward reaction (better yield, around 98% at room temperature), but the rate would be too slow to be economical. Higher temperatures speed up the reaction but reduce yield. 450°C is a compromise — an acceptable yield (around 15–25%) at a commercially viable rate.

Pressure — more moles on the left: on the left there are 4 moles of gas (1 N2 + 3 H2); on the right there are 2 moles (2 NH3). By Le Chatelier’s principle, high pressure shifts equilibrium to the right (fewer moles of gas). Very high pressures give better yields but are extremely expensive and dangerous to maintain. 200 atmospheres is again a compromise: a high enough pressure to be practical without prohibitive engineering costs.

Iron catalyst: lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the system reaches equilibrium faster without changing the position of equilibrium. It does not improve yield, only rate.

Because the yield per pass is only around 15–25%, the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are separated from the ammonia and recycled back into the reactor. The ammonia is cooled and liquefied (it has a higher boiling point than N2 and H2), allowing the unreacted gases to remain as gas and be pumped back. Overall efficiency is very high despite the low single-pass yield.

Ammonia and Fertilisers (Triple-only)

Ammonia manufactured by the Haber process is used to make nitrogen-based fertilisers. Ammonia can be oxidised to form nitric acid, which then reacts with more ammonia to make ammonium nitrate, a widely used fertiliser. NPK fertilisers contain nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium in ratios designed to optimise crop growth. They are formulated by combining ammonium salts with phosphate and potassium compounds.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The Haber process is a classic exam context for Le Chatelier’s principle. When explaining why 450°C is chosen, you must address both rate and yield — stating only one will lose marks. Remember: the catalyst does NOT change the position of equilibrium or the yield; it only speeds up attainment of equilibrium. For equilibrium questions, always state which direction the equilibrium shifts AND why, linking clearly to Le Chatelier’s principle.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal, concentrations are constant, and both reactions continue. Equilibrium is dynamic, not static.
  • Le Chatelier’s principle: any change in conditions shifts equilibrium to partially oppose that change. Temperature changes affect yield; catalysts only affect rate.
  • The Haber process makes ammonia from N2 and H2 at 450°C and 200 atm with an iron catalyst — a compromise between yield and rate. Unreacted gases are recycled.

Catalyst noted as speeding up equilibrium without changing yield. All reasoning linked to Le Chatelier's principle.

lessons.title: Crude Oil, Hydrocarbons and Cracking
lessons.description: Fractional distillation, alkanes and alkenes, combustion, cracking and atmospheric pollutants.
lessons.content_html:
Crude Oil and Hydrocarbons

Crude oil is a finite resource that took millions of years to form from the compressed remains of ancient marine organisms. It is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons — molecules containing only hydrogen and carbon. Because crude oil is a mixture rather than a pure compound, its components can be separated without a chemical reaction.

Fractional Distillation

Crude oil is separated into useful fractions (groups of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points) by fractional distillation. The crude oil is heated in a furnace until most of it vaporises. The vapour enters a tall fractionating column that is hot at the bottom (>350°C) and cool at the top (<25°C). Hydrocarbons condense when they reach their boiling point:

  • Top of column: petrol (gasoline) and gases — small molecules, low boiling point.
  • Middle: kerosene (aviation fuel), diesel.
  • Bottom: heavy fuel oil and bitumen — large molecules, very high boiling point.
Key Fact

In fractional distillation, smaller hydrocarbons have lower boiling points and are collected near the top of the column. They are also less viscous (flow more easily) and more flammable. Larger hydrocarbons have higher boiling points, greater viscosity, and are less flammable.

Alkanes

Most hydrocarbons in crude oil are alkanes. They have the general formula \(C_nH_{2n+2}\) and are described as saturated because they contain only single C—C bonds. The first four alkanes are:

  • Methane: \(CH_4\) (natural gas)
  • Ethane: \(C_2H_6\)
  • Propane: \(C_3H_8\)
  • Butane: \(C_4H_{10}\)

As the carbon chain length increases, boiling point and viscosity increase, while flammability decreases. These trends are caused by stronger intermolecular forces between larger molecules.

Combustion of Hydrocarbons

When hydrocarbons burn in a plentiful supply of oxygen, complete combustion occurs, producing only carbon dioxide and water:

$$C_nH_{2n+2} + \frac{3n+1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow nCO_2 + (n+1)H_2O$$

For example, for methane: \(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\). This releases large amounts of energy, making hydrocarbons valuable fuels.

When oxygen supply is limited, incomplete combustion occurs, producing toxic carbon monoxide (CO) and/or carbon particles (soot). Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless but dangerously toxic — it binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells, preventing oxygen transport.

Burning hydrocarbon fuels also releases other pollutants:

  • Sulfur dioxide (SO2): produced when sulfur impurities in fuels burn. Dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, which damages buildings, soils, and aquatic ecosystems.
  • Nitrogen oxides (NOₓ): formed when nitrogen and oxygen in the air react at the high temperatures inside engines. Also contribute to acid rain and the formation of photochemical smog.
  • Carbon dioxide: a greenhouse gas — its increasing concentration in the atmosphere contributes to global warming.
Key Fact

Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide (toxic) and soot. Sulfur impurities produce SO2 (acid rain). High-temperature combustion produces nitrogen oxides (acid rain, smog). Carbon dioxide causes global warming.

Cracking

Cracking is used to break long-chain hydrocarbons (plentiful but less useful) into shorter-chain hydrocarbons that are in higher demand. Cracking always produces at least one alkene — a hydrocarbon with a C=C double bond. Alkenes have the general formula \(C_nH_{2n}\).

Catalytic cracking: long-chain hydrocarbons are vaporised and passed over a heated aluminium oxide (or zeolite) catalyst at around 500°C. The catalyst lowers the activation energy and allows cracking at a lower temperature. Produces mainly branched-chain alkanes and aromatic compounds, useful for petrol.

Thermal cracking (steam cracking): carried out at very high temperatures (around 850°C) and high pressure using steam. Produces a higher proportion of alkenes (especially ethene, \(C_2H_4\)), which are used as monomers to make plastics and polymers.

A simple example of cracking: a long alkane such as decane can be cracked into octane (a petrol component) and ethene: \(C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_8H_{18} + C_2H_4\).

Testing for Alkenes

Alkenes can be distinguished from alkanes using bromine water. Alkenes decolourise bromine water (orange to colourless) because the C=C double bond reacts with bromine in an addition reaction. Alkanes do not react with bromine water under normal conditions, so the orange colour remains.

Exam Focus: Fractions and Cracking

When answering questions on fractional distillation, remember that shorter hydrocarbon chains have lower boiling points, are more volatile, flow more easily, and ignite more readily. Cracking serves the dual purpose of increasing the supply of shorter, more useful fractions and producing alkenes as raw materials for polymer manufacture. Thermal cracking uses very high temperatures and pressures; catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst at lower temperatures — be precise about which conditions apply to each method in your exam answers.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing combustion equations, check that your equation is balanced and that you specify whether oxygen supply is limited (incomplete) or excess (complete). For pollutant questions, name the specific gas AND give its environmental impact — ‘it pollutes the air’ earns no marks. For cracking questions, remember: every cracking reaction produces at least one alkene. Bromine water test: decolourises with alkene, stays orange with alkane.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons separated by fractional distillation. Smaller fractions (top of column) have lower boiling points and higher flammability; larger fractions (bottom) have higher boiling points and greater viscosity.
  • Complete combustion produces CO2 and water. Incomplete combustion produces CO (toxic) and soot. Sulfur impurities give SO2 (acid rain); high temperatures produce NOₓ (acid rain, smog).
  • Cracking breaks large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes. Alkenes are unsaturated (C=C bond), decolourise bromine water, and are used to make polymers.

lessons.title: Tests for Ions, Gases and Chromatography
lessons.description: Flame tests, hydroxide tests, gas tests, chromatography Rf values and instrumental analysis.
lessons.content_html:
Identifying Substances in Chemistry

Chemists use a range of analytical techniques to identify unknown substances. These range from simple laboratory tests — such as flame tests and gas tests — to instrumental methods such as the flame photometer. This lesson covers the key tests you need to know, many of which are Triple-only content that goes beyond the Combined Science course.

Flame Tests

A flame test is used to detect the presence of certain metal ions. A clean nichrome wire loop is dipped in the sample and held in a Bunsen flame. Different metal ions produce characteristic flame colours:

  • Lithium (Li&sup+;): crimson / red
  • Sodium (Na&sup+;): bright yellow
  • Potassium (K&sup+;): lilac
  • Calcium (Ca²+;): orange-red
  • Copper (Cu²+;): green
Key Fact

Flame test colours: lithium = crimson, sodium = yellow, potassium = lilac, calcium = orange-red, copper = green. Sodium’s yellow is so intense it can mask other colours — the wire must be thoroughly cleaned between tests.

Tests for Metal Ions Using Sodium Hydroxide

Many metal ions form insoluble hydroxide precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added. The colour of the precipitate identifies the metal ion:

  • Copper (Cu²+;): blue precipitate
  • Iron(II) (Fe²+;): green precipitate
  • Iron(III) (Fe³+;): brown (rust-coloured) precipitate
  • Calcium (Ca²+;): white precipitate
  • Aluminium (Al³+;): white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH

Adding sodium hydroxide solution to an ammonium salt and gently warming releases ammonia gas (NH3). Ammonia can be detected by holding damp red litmus paper near the mouth of the tube — it turns blue because ammonia is an alkaline gas. This is the definitive test for the ammonium ion (NH4&sup+;).

Gas Tests

Four gases are commonly tested in GCSE chemistry. Each has a specific test and result:

Hydrogen (H2): hold a lit splint to the mouth of the test tube — a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen.

Oxygen (O2): hold a glowing splint to the mouth of the tube — oxygen relights (re-ignites) the splint.

Carbon dioxide (CO2): bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) — it turns milky white (cloudy) as calcium carbonate precipitates.

Chlorine (Cl2): hold damp litmus paper in the gas — it is first turned red (acid) then bleached white. Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas with a pungent smell.

Key Fact

Gas tests: hydrogen — squeaky pop with lit splint. Oxygen — relights glowing splint. Carbon dioxide — turns limewater milky. Chlorine — bleaches damp litmus paper.

Chromatography

Chromatography separates mixtures based on the relative solubility of each component in a solvent. In paper chromatography, a spot of mixture is placed on a pencil baseline on chromatography paper. The paper is placed in a small volume of solvent (below the baseline), which travels up the paper by capillary action, carrying dissolved components with it. Components that are more soluble in the solvent travel further.

Calculating Rf Values

The Rf value (retention factor) is calculated as:

$$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$$

Rf values are always between 0 and 1. Each substance has a characteristic Rf value in a specific solvent at a specific temperature. A pure substance produces a single spot; a mixture produces multiple spots. Unknown substances can be identified by comparing their Rf values with known reference values run on the same chromatogram.

The solvent front travels 8.0 cm. A dye spot travels 6.4 cm. Calculate the Rf value.

$$R_f = \frac{6.4}{8.0} = 0.80$$

The dye has an Rf value of 0.80 in this solvent. Always measure to the centre of the spot from the pencil baseline, not from the bottom of the paper.

Instrumental Analysis: The Flame Photometer

The flame photometer is an instrumental technique that identifies metal ions by analysing the specific wavelengths of light they emit when placed in a flame. It is far more sensitive than a manual flame test and can detect and measure the concentration of metal ions in very dilute solutions. Flame photometry is used in hospitals to measure sodium and potassium ion concentrations in blood and urine samples, and in agriculture to analyse soil mineral content.

For the exam, learn flame test colours precisely: lithium gives crimson, sodium gives yellow, potassium gives lilac, calcium gives orange-red, and copper gives blue-green. A common error is confusing the white precipitate from aluminium or calcium ions with that from magnesium: adding excess sodium hydroxide dissolves the aluminium hydroxide precipitate but not the magnesium hydroxide, which lets you distinguish them reliably in an exam question.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Flame test and gas test questions require precise language — ‘it goes white’ for limewater is incomplete; state ‘turns milky/cloudy white’. For the chlorine test, mention both actions: turns red then bleaches. When calculating Rf values, always measure from the baseline (pencil line) to the centre of the spot, not from the bottom of the paper. Rf values must be between 0 and 1 — if yours is above 1, you’ve divided incorrectly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Flame tests identify metal ions by characteristic colours: lithium (crimson), sodium (yellow), potassium (lilac), calcium (orange-red), copper (green). Sodium hydroxide precipitates can also distinguish metal ions.
  • Gas tests: hydrogen = squeaky pop; oxygen = relights glowing splint; CO2 = milky limewater; chlorine = bleaches damp litmus. Ammonia turns damp red litmus blue.
  • Chromatography separates mixtures; Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent. The flame photometer provides sensitive, quantitative identification of metal ions.

lessons.title: Earth's Atmosphere and Climate Change
lessons.description: How Earth's atmosphere evolved, modern composition, greenhouse gases and climate change.
lessons.content_html:
The Early Atmosphere

For the first billion years of Earth’s history, the atmosphere was very different from today. Scientists believe it was dominated by carbon dioxide, with very little or no oxygen. It also contained water vapour, nitrogen, and small amounts of methane and ammonia. This early atmosphere was produced by intense volcanic activity, which released gases trapped inside the planet.

As the Earth cooled, the water vapour in the atmosphere condensed to form the early oceans. This removed a large amount of water vapour from the atmosphere. Scientists draw comparisons with the present-day atmospheres of Venus and Mars, which are still dominated by carbon dioxide — supporting the model of what Earth’s early atmosphere may have looked like.

Key Fact

The early atmosphere: mainly CO2, plus water vapour, nitrogen, and traces of methane and ammonia. As the planet cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans. Volcanic activity was the source of most of these gases.

How the Atmosphere Changed

Over billions of years, the composition of the atmosphere changed dramatically, primarily due to the evolution of life and the formation of the oceans:

1. Photosynthesis by early organisms: the first photosynthetic organisms (simple algae and cyanobacteria) evolved in the oceans. They used carbon dioxide from the water and atmosphere, releasing oxygen as a waste product. Over hundreds of millions of years, oxygen levels in the atmosphere slowly increased.

2. Oceans absorbing CO2: carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans, where it reacted to form carbonates. These were deposited as carbonate rocks such as limestone, and became part of the shells and skeletons of marine organisms. This locked up vast quantities of carbon dioxide in solid rock — removing it from the atmosphere.

3. Formation of the ozone layer: as oxygen levels rose, some oxygen molecules were converted to ozone (O3) in the upper atmosphere. The ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun. Its formation allowed more complex life to evolve on land without being damaged by UV radiation.

The Modern Atmosphere

Today’s atmosphere has been roughly stable for around 200 million years. Its approximate composition by volume is:

  • Nitrogen (N2): approximately 78%
  • Oxygen (O2): approximately 21%
  • Other gases (mainly argon, plus very small amounts of carbon dioxide and water vapour): approximately 1%
Key Fact

Modern atmosphere: approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and about 1% other gases (mainly argon). Carbon dioxide makes up approximately 0.04% — a very small proportion, but it has a disproportionately large effect on climate.

The Greenhouse Effect

The Sun emits energy as short-wavelength radiation (mainly visible light), which passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface. The warm surface emits longer-wavelength infrared radiation. This infrared radiation is absorbed by greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which then re-emit the energy in all directions — including back towards Earth. This natural greenhouse effect is essential for life — without it, the average surface temperature would be far below zero.

Carbon dioxide (CO2): released by burning fossil fuels, deforestation (removing trees that absorb CO2), and cement production. Its concentration in the atmosphere has been rising significantly since the Industrial Revolution.

Methane (CH4): released from livestock (digestive processes), landfill sites (decomposition of organic waste), and rice paddy fields. Methane is a more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 over a short timescale, though it breaks down in the atmosphere more quickly.

Water vapour (H2O): a naturally occurring greenhouse gas and the most abundant one, though its concentration is largely governed by temperature rather than direct human activity.

Human Impact and Climate Change

Human activities have significantly increased the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, particularly carbon dioxide and methane. The scientific consensus, supported by many independent lines of evidence, is that this enhanced global warming is causing climate change. Evidence includes rising average global temperatures, retreating glaciers and ice caps, rising sea levels, and shifts in the timing of seasons and species distribution.

Predicted consequences of continued climate change include: more frequent and severe extreme weather events (droughts, floods, storms); rising sea levels threatening low-lying coastal areas; disruption to food and water supplies; loss of biodiversity as ecosystems shift or collapse.

Responses include: reducing fossil fuel use and transitioning to renewable energy sources; increasing energy efficiency; carbon capture and storage; international agreements to limit emissions. The challenge is balancing economic development with environmental protection — particularly for developing nations.

Key Fact

The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm; without it, life could not exist. Human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture) are increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, enhancing the greenhouse effect and causing measurable global warming and climate change.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on climate change reward precise scientific reasoning. When explaining the greenhouse effect, use the correct sequence: Sun emits short-wavelength radiation → Earth’s surface absorbs it and warms → surface emits infrared radiation → greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared, some back to Earth. Do not confuse the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion (a separate topic). For human impact questions, name specific activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation) and specific gases (CO2, CH4) rather than giving vague answers about ‘pollution’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The early atmosphere was mainly CO2. Photosynthesis by early organisms increased O2. Ocean absorption and carbonate formation removed CO2. Today’s atmosphere is approximately 78% N2, 21% O2, 1% other gases.
  • The greenhouse effect: greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, water vapour) absorb infrared radiation emitted by Earth’s surface and re-emit it, keeping the planet warm. This process is natural and essential for life.
  • Human activities are increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, enhancing the greenhouse effect and causing global warming and climate change, supported by multiple independent lines of scientific evidence.

lessons.content_html:
Alkanes and Alkenes

Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms. Alkanes are saturated — every carbon atom is bonded to as many hydrogen atoms as possible. Alkenes are unsaturated, containing at least one carbon—carbon double bond.

The distinction matters because the double bond in alkenes is chemically reactive. You can test for an alkene using bromine water: alkenes decolourise the orange solution to colourless because bromine adds across the double bond. Alkanes do not react, so the bromine water stays orange.

Key Fact

Alkanes are saturated (single C—C bonds) and do not decolourise bromine water. Alkenes are unsaturated (contain a C=C double bond) and do decolourise bromine water from orange to colourless.

Addition Polymerisation

Addition polymerisation occurs when alkene monomers react together to form a polymer. The double bond in each monomer opens up to join the chain. No other product is formed. A simple example is ethene (\(\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CH}_2\)) polymerising to form poly(ethene):

$$n\, \text{CH}_2{=}\text{CH}_2 \rightarrow \text{---}(\text{CH}_2\text{---}\text{CH}_2)_n\text{---}$$

The monomer is written inside brackets with a double bond; the polymer is shown with the repeat unit inside brackets and the subscript n indicating many thousands of units. Other addition polymers include poly(propene) and poly(chloroethene) (PVC).

To draw an addition polymer from a monomer: (1) remove the double bond; (2) draw a single bond on each side of the two carbons that formed the double bond; (3) add a bracket around the repeat unit with bonds crossing each bracket; (4) add subscript n. To identify the monomer from a polymer: reverse the process — add the double bond back between the two carbons in the repeat unit.

Condensation Polymerisation

Condensation polymerisation links monomers that each have two functional groups. Each time two monomers join, a small molecule — usually water — is eliminated. Unlike addition polymerisation, the monomers do not need a double bond.

Two important condensation polymers are polyesters and polyamides. Polyesters form ester links (—COO—) between a diol and a dicarboxylic acid. Polyamides form amide links (—CONH—) between a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid. Nylon is a well-known polyamide.

Key Fact

Addition polymerisation: monomers have C=C double bonds; no other product. Condensation polymerisation: monomers have two functional groups; small molecule (usually water) released at each link. Polyesters and nylon are condensation polymers.

Alcohols

Alcohols form a homologous series. All alcohols contain the hydroxyl (—OH) functional group. The first four members are methanol, ethanol, propanol, and butanol. Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is the most important for GCSE: it is the alcohol in drinks, and it is widely used as a fuel and solvent.

Ethanol can be made in two ways: by reacting ethene with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst (hydration — industrial process, uses a finite resource), or by fermentation of sugars using yeast.

In fermentation, yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide under anaerobic (oxygen-free) conditions and at an optimum temperature of around 25–35 °C:

$$\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}$$ $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{CO}_2$$

The ethanol concentration cannot rise above about 12–15% because higher concentrations kill the yeast. To obtain pure ethanol, the mixture is distilled. Fermentation uses a renewable resource (sugar) and happens at room temperature, making it lower energy than industrial hydration.

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain the —COOH functional group. They are weak acids — they partially ionise in water. The first members are methanoic acid, ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH), propanoic acid, and butanoic acid. Ethanoic acid is found in vinegar.

Carboxylic acids react with carbonates to produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide. They also react with alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst to form esters and water. Esters have fruity smells and are used as food flavourings and perfumes.

In this core practical, a spirit burner containing a known mass of alcohol is used to heat a measured volume of water in a calorimeter. The temperature rise of the water is recorded. Key variables to control: mass of water, draught conditions, distance between flame and calorimeter. The energy released is calculated using \(Q = mc\Delta T\), where \(m\) is the mass of water, \(c\) is the specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J/g°C), and \(\Delta T\) is the temperature change. The mass of alcohol burned (from the change in mass of the spirit burner) gives the energy per gram.

Limitations include heat loss to surroundings, incomplete combustion, and evaporation of alcohol. These mean the experimental value is lower than the standard enthalpy of combustion. Repeats and averaging reduce random error.

Recycling Polymers

Most addition polymers are non-biodegradable, meaning they persist in the environment for centuries. This creates significant waste problems. Polymers can be recycled mechanically (sorting, melting, re-moulding) or by chemical methods such as cracking back into monomers. Some condensation polymers (e.g. polyesters) can be chemically recycled more easily than addition polymers.

Alternatively, some polymers can be used as a fuel by incineration, recovering some energy. However, this releases carbon dioxide and may release harmful gases if chlorine-containing plastics like PVC are burned. Biodegradable plastics (bioplastics made from plant materials) offer a more sustainable future but currently have higher production costs and limited mechanical strength.

Key Fact

Non-biodegradable polymers persist in landfill and oceans for centuries. Solutions include mechanical recycling, chemical recycling (cracking), incineration (energy recovery but CO₂ released), and biodegradable bioplastics (sustainable but costly).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 3-mark ‘Describe’ question on addition polymerisation, you need: (1) monomers have a C=C double bond; (2) the double bond opens; (3) monomers join to form a long chain with no other product. For 4-mark ‘Compare’ questions on addition vs condensation polymerisation, make sure you contrast both the type of monomer needed and whether a small molecule is produced — a single-sided answer will lose marks. In extended-response questions on sustainability, link polymer properties (non-biodegradable) to the environmental impact, then evaluate recycling methods with their trade-offs to reach the higher mark bands.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Alkenes have a C=C double bond and decolourise bromine water; alkanes do not. Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers; condensation polymerisation joins bifunctional monomers, releasing water, producing polyesters (ester links) and polyamides (amide links).
  • Ethanol is made by fermentation of sugars by yeast (renewable, room temperature) or by hydration of ethene (industrial, finite resource). Carboxylic acids contain —COOH, are weak acids, and react with alcohols to form esters.
  • Non-biodegradable polymers cause environmental problems; solutions include mechanical recycling, chemical recycling, incineration, and bioplastics — each with advantages and disadvantages.

lessons.title: Nanoparticles, Materials and Composites
lessons.description: Nanoparticle properties and risks, glass, ceramics, alloys, and composite materials for GCSE Chemistry.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Nanoparticles?

Nanoparticles are structures that measure between 1 and 100 nanometres (nm) in at least one dimension. One nanometre is 10-9 m — far smaller than a human hair (~80 000 nm wide). By comparison, fine particles (used in older applications such as talcum powder) are typically 100 nm–2500 nm, and bulk materials are larger still.

Nanoparticles are not a new phenomenon: soot from candles and carbon black in ancient ink contain nanoparticles. What is new is the ability to engineer them precisely and exploit their unusual properties.

Key Fact

Nanoparticles: 1–100 nm. Fine particles: 100–2500 nm. Bulk materials: larger. A nanometre is one billionth of a metre. The extremely small size of nanoparticles gives them unique properties not seen in the same material in bulk form.

Surface Area to Volume Ratio

The key reason nanoparticles behave differently from bulk materials is their very high surface area to volume ratio. As a particle is made smaller, the proportion of atoms on the surface compared to those in the interior increases dramatically. Surface atoms are more reactive because they have unsatisfied bonds — so a higher surface area to volume ratio means greater chemical reactivity.

Imagine cutting a large cube into tiny cubes: the total surface area increases while the total volume stays the same. This principle is why nanoparticles of gold, silver, and titanium dioxide behave very differently from the same substances in their visible (bulk) forms.

A cube of side 4 cm: surface area = 6 × 42 = 96 cm2; volume = 43 = 64 cm3; ratio = 96/64 = 1.5 cm-1

Split into 64 cubes of side 1 cm each: total surface area = 64 × 6 = 384 cm2; total volume = 64 cm3; ratio = 384/64 = 6 cm-1 — four times larger. Reducing particle size dramatically increases surface area to volume ratio, explaining why nanoparticles are much more reactive than bulk material.

Applications of Nanoparticles

Nanoparticles are exploited across many fields because of their enhanced properties:

  • Sunscreen: titanium dioxide and zinc oxide nanoparticles absorb and scatter ultraviolet radiation more effectively than bulk particles of the same materials. Their tiny size also makes them transparent on skin rather than leaving a white film.
  • Medicine: nanoparticles can be engineered to carry drugs directly to cancer cells, reducing side effects compared with conventional chemotherapy. Silver nanoparticles have antimicrobial properties and are incorporated into wound dressings and clothing.
  • Electronics: nanoparticles enable smaller, faster components. Carbon nanotubes have very high tensile strength and electrical conductivity, making them valuable in advanced electronics and structural materials.
  • Catalysis: nanoparticle catalysts (e.g. platinum nanoparticles in catalytic converters) provide a much larger surface area for reactions to occur, improving efficiency.

Risks and the Precautionary Principle

The same properties that make nanoparticles useful also raise concerns. Their tiny size means they can penetrate biological barriers — entering cells, crossing the blood–brain barrier, or accumulating in organs — in ways that larger particles of the same material cannot. The long-term health effects are still being researched, and some nanoparticles have been shown to cause inflammation or cellular damage in laboratory studies.

Because the full risks are not yet understood, scientists and regulators apply the precautionary principle: taking protective measures before harms are proven, rather than waiting for certainty. This means using nanoparticles only where benefits clearly outweigh the risks, and continuing active research.

Key Fact

Nanoparticles can cross biological membranes due to their tiny size, potentially causing harm. The precautionary principle says: act cautiously when risks are uncertain. Their high surface area also makes them more chemically reactive than bulk particles of the same substance.

Properties of Glass and Ceramics

Soda glass is made by melting silicon dioxide (sand) with sodium carbonate and limestone. It is transparent, hard, and chemically resistant, but brittle and has a relatively low melting point. Borosilicate glass contains boron trioxide, giving it a much higher melting point and resistance to thermal shock — it is used in laboratory glassware and ovenproof dishes.

Clay ceramics such as pottery and bricks are made by shaping clay and firing it at high temperatures. They are very hard, brittle, and chemically inert. Their crystalline structure makes them good thermal and electrical insulators.

Metals, Alloys and Composites

Pure metals have regular, closely packed crystal structures, allowing layers of atoms to slide over each other — making them malleable. Adding another element creates an alloy, where the different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, making it harder for them to slide. This is why alloys are generally stronger and harder than pure metals. Steel (iron + carbon), brass (copper + zinc), and bronze (copper + tin) are common examples.

A composite material combines materials so that each contributes its best property. Glass-fibre-reinforced polymer (GFRP, or fibreglass) combines glass fibres (stiff and strong) embedded in a polymer resin (lightweight). Carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CFRP) uses carbon fibres, giving even higher stiffness and strength at low mass. Both are used in sports equipment, aircraft bodies, and boat hulls where a high strength-to-weight ratio is needed.

GFRP (fibreglass): glass fibres in a polymer matrix. Strong, lightweight, corrosion-resistant, and relatively cheap. Used in boat hulls, car body panels, and insulation.

CFRP (carbon fibre): carbon fibres in a polymer matrix. Stronger and stiffer than GFRP, with a lower density, but significantly more expensive to produce. Used in racing car chassis, aerospace components, and high-performance sports equipment (bicycles, golf clubs).

The key principle for both: the composite exploits the stiffness of the fibres and the toughness of the polymer matrix, achieving properties neither material has on its own.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about nanoparticles, always link their properties to surface area to volume ratio — this is the examiner’s expected mechanism. If asked to ‘explain why nanoparticles are more reactive,’ you must say ‘higher surface area to volume ratio, so more atoms are exposed on the surface.’ For material selection questions (4–6 marks), compare two materials explicitly: name a property of each, explain why that property matters for the application, and state which is better suited. Avoid vague answers like ‘stronger’ — say what it is stronger than and why that matters.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Nanoparticles are 1–100 nm in size. Their very high surface area to volume ratio makes them more reactive than bulk materials, enabling uses in sunscreen, medicine, electronics, and catalysis — but also raising health concerns addressed by the precautionary principle.
  • Glass (soda and borosilicate) and clay ceramics are hard, brittle, and chemically resistant. Alloys are harder than pure metals because different-sized atoms disrupt the regular crystal layers.
  • Composite materials like GFRP and CFRP combine fibres and polymer matrices to produce materials with superior strength-to-weight ratios, suitable for aerospace, marine, and sports applications.

lessons.title: Earth's Resources, Potable Water and Life-Cycle Assessment
lessons.description: Finite vs renewable resources, potable water treatment, desalination, recycling, and life-cycle assessment.
lessons.content_html:
Natural Resources and Sustainability

Humans use the Earth’s natural resources to meet needs for warmth, shelter, food, and transport. Some resources are finite — they are being consumed faster than nature can replace them. Others are renewable — they replenish naturally and will not run out if managed carefully.

Sustainable development means meeting present needs without preventing future generations from meeting theirs. Chemistry contributes by finding alternatives to finite resources (biofuels, bioplastics), improving recycling, and designing more efficient processes that generate less waste.

Key Fact

Finite resources (e.g. fossil fuels, metal ores) will eventually run out. Renewable resources (e.g. timber, cotton, solar energy) replenish naturally. Sustainable development balances today’s needs with preserving resources for future generations.

Potable Water

Potable water is safe to drink. It is not pure water (which contains only H2O); it may contain low levels of dissolved minerals but must be free from harmful microorganisms and toxic substances. In the United Kingdom, most potable water comes from fresh water sources — rivers and reservoirs — and is treated before distribution.

The treatment of fresh water involves three main steps:

  1. Sedimentation: the water is allowed to stand in settlement tanks. Larger particles and fine debris sink to the bottom as sediment.
  2. Filtration: the water passes through filter beds of sand and gravel to remove smaller suspended particles, producing clear water.
  3. Chlorination: a controlled amount of chlorine is added to kill bacteria and other pathogens, making the water safe to drink.
Key Fact

UK potable water treatment: (1) sedimentation — particles settle; (2) filtration through sand/gravel — removes suspended particles; (3) chlorination — kills bacteria. The water is safe to drink but is not chemically pure.

Desalination

In regions where fresh water is scarce, desalination is used to convert sea water into potable water. Two main methods are used:

  • Distillation: sea water is boiled; the steam (water vapour) condenses and is collected as pure water, leaving the salts behind. This requires large amounts of energy.
  • Reverse osmosis: sea water is forced under high pressure through a membrane that blocks salt ions but allows water molecules through. This also requires significant energy input.

Treating fresh water from rivers and reservoirs (UK approach) is relatively low-cost and uses less energy because the water is already fresh and only needs sedimentation, filtration, and chlorination.

Desalination removes dissolved salts from sea water — a much more energy-intensive process. However, for countries with limited rainfall and no major rivers (e.g. parts of the Middle East), desalination is essential. The high energy cost also means higher carbon emissions unless renewable energy sources are used.

Waste Water Treatment

Used water from homes, hospitals, and industry is called waste water (sewage). It must be treated before being returned to rivers or the sea. The main stages of sewage treatment are: (1) screening — large solids are removed by metal screens; (2) sedimentation — fine suspended solids settle as sludge; (3) biological treatment — aerobic bacteria break down organic matter in the liquid effluent; (4) anaerobic digestion of sludge — the separated sludge is digested by bacteria in the absence of oxygen, releasing biogas (mainly methane), which can be used as a fuel.

Recycling and Waste Reduction

Recycling conserves finite resources by recovering materials from waste products rather than extracting new raw materials. It generally requires less energy than extracting and processing virgin materials, and it reduces the volume of waste sent to landfill.

However, recycling is not without cost. Collection, sorting, transport, and reprocessing all require energy and produce some waste. Some materials (such as mixed plastics or composite materials) are difficult to recycle cost-effectively. Despite these challenges, recycling plays a vital role in sustainable development — particularly for metals such as aluminium, where the energy saving over primary production is very large compared to extracting fresh aluminium from its ore by electrolysis.

Life-Cycle Assessment

A life-cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life:

  1. Extracting and processing raw materials — energy used, land disturbed, waste generated.
  2. Manufacturing and packaging — energy and chemicals consumed in production.
  3. Using the product — energy consumed during use; repairs and maintenance.
  4. End-of-life disposal — whether the product goes to landfill, is incinerated (releasing CO2), or is recycled.

LCAs involve value judgements, making them potentially subjective. Different companies or researchers may choose to include different stages, use different data sources, or weight environmental impacts differently. For example, a manufacturer might minimise the extraction stage in their own product’s LCA but scrutinise it heavily for a competitor.

LCA results are most reliable when conducted by independent bodies using agreed methodologies. Students should note that LCA data can be presented selectively and should evaluate the source of any LCA before accepting its conclusions.

Key Fact

An LCA covers four stages: (1) raw material extraction; (2) manufacturing and packaging; (3) use of the product; (4) disposal (landfill, incineration, or recycling). LCAs can be subjective depending on what data is included and how impacts are weighted.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on potable water treatment often ask you to ‘describe’ or ‘explain’ the stages. Make sure you give them in order (sedimentation → filtration → chlorination) and state what each stage does, not just what it is called. For LCA evaluation questions (6 marks), the top band requires you to comment on the limitations of LCAs (subjectivity, selective data) as well as their usefulness — a one-sided answer capping the mark at Secure. For ‘compare desalination with UK fresh water treatment’ questions, always mention energy cost as the key distinguishing factor.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Finite resources (fossil fuels, metal ores) will run out; renewable resources replenish naturally. Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations.
  • UK potable water: sedimentation → filtration → chlorination. Desalination (distillation or reverse osmosis) converts sea water to potable water but requires significantly more energy.
  • A life-cycle assessment evaluates environmental impact across extraction, manufacture, use, and disposal. Recycling reduces use of finite resources but LCAs can be subjective; evaluate the source before accepting conclusions.

practice_questions.text: A local council is deciding whether to supply water using a new desalination plant or by expanding its existing reservoir and water treatment works. Evaluate the two options, considering environmental impact, cost, and reliability of water supply.

practice_questions.text: Recycling aluminium uses considerably less energy than producing it from its ore. Using this example, explain the benefits of recycling finite resources. In your answer, consider both the environmental and economic arguments.

Secure: Two or more benefits with explanation; limited acknowledgement of drawbacks.
Developing: Benefits listed without clear explanation or linkage to aluminium.
Emerging: Simple points.

• Recycling reduces need to mine (extract) more ore [1]

• Reduced CO₂ emissions from energy production [1]
• Less waste to landfill [1]

glossary_terms.definition: Materials from the Earth used by humans, including water, minerals, fossil fuels and the atmosphere; some are finite, others are renewable.
Resources used faster than they can be replaced, which will eventually run out, such as fossil fuels and metal ores.
Resources replaced at the same rate as they are used, so they will not run out, such as timber, cotton, and solar energy.
Development that meets the needs of today's people without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Water safe to drink; not the same as pure water, as it still contains low levels of dissolved substances, but free from harmful microorganisms.
The process of removing dissolved salts from sea water or salty water to produce potable water, using distillation or reverse osmosis.
Collecting and reprocessing waste materials to produce new products, conserving finite resources and reducing landfill.
An assessment of the environmental impact of a product across its entire lifetime: raw material extraction, manufacture, use, and disposal or recycling.
